Should New Airbnbs Be Limited In Logan Square, Humboldt Park? Residents Can Weigh In On Ballot

There are about 108 Airbnbs in the ward, a higher concentration than citywide rentals. Resident feedback could prompt policy to limit new Airbnbs in the area.
by Ariel Parrella-Aureli 22 hours agoOctober 29, 2026

HUMBOLDT PARK — Residents in the 26th Ward will be asked on next week’s ballot to weigh in on whether they think there should be a cap placed on new vacation rentals in the area.

Ald. Jessie Fuentes (26th) is asking constituents in her ward, which covers most of Humboldt Park and parts of Logan Square, Hermosa and Belmont Cragin, whether there should be a limit on new vacation rentals like Airbnbs and VRBO apartments in the ward to instead keep apartments available to area residents amid Chicago’s rental housing shortage.

The non-binding referendum question, for 26th Ward residents only, will gauge voter support for a policy proposal around limiting new short-term rental vacation apartments in the ward, or specific areas of it. It’s one of five non-binding questions Chicago voters will see on their ballot, which are votes not tied to a specific policy.

“The idea is that if neighbors are saying we should limit these and focus on keeping these units to be housing for individuals, then we would then subsequently draft legislation that would limit Airbnbs in the precincts,” Fuentes said.

Airbnbs have heavily saturated the Northwest Side, particularly in Logan Square, Humboldt Park, Wicker Park and Avondale — areas popular with visitors but without as many hotels as other neighborhoods.

In the 26th Ward, there are about 108 active Airbnbs rentals, a higher concentration than citywide rentals, Fuentes said.

Since 2023, the supply for short-term housing rentals has increased in Logan Square, Avondale and parts of Humboldt Park, peaking earlier this year, according to available data from AirDNA, an analytics site that tracks data and market trends from Airbnb, VRBO and Booking.com rentals.

Airbnb listings account for 44 percent of short-term rentals in the three neighborhoods, compared to 13.5 percent of bookings from VRBO, according to AirDNA.

There are close to 100 short-term listings from the three sites in Humboldt Park, about 110 in Avondale, seven in Hermosa and 450 in Logan Square, per the insight website, though some include duplicate listings advertised on multiple rental sites.

Should 26th Ward voters want to see a cap on new vacation rentals, Fuentes said she would then work to draft legislation for the issue. The legislation would not impact current Airbnbs. Existing vacation rentals “went through the proper licensing process, and we want to respect that,” Fuentes said.

Last year, a group of City Council members tried unsuccessfully to get an updated ordinance passed that would give alderpeople more power to ban short-term vacation rentals on a precinct basis over concerns of “bad operators,” an issue in various wards including the 26th Ward, Fuentes said.

But while the measure stalled, various alderpeople have still been able to ban vacation rentals this year in certain precincts under an existing ordinance allowing for such bans with a petition signed by 25 percent of the precinct′s registered voters.

Fuentes said she’d consider using the same tool after getting feedback from voters via the referendum.

“We have residents who have come [to us] with some serious concerns, not just about parties and things of that nature — I think we can all expect, to some level, that happens across the city — but some instances bring violence to our communities and those individuals don’t live here, so they don’t have to grapple with the fallout of what that means for the community,” she said.

An Airbnb spokesperson said the company is against “any proposal that strips responsible Chicago residents of their right to share their homes and takes away income that helps Chicago families afford to stay in their homes” and that company hosts contribute millions to the local economy.

According to data provided by the company, the typical Airbnb host in the 26th Ward earned approximately $17,000 last year, income that nearly 60 percent of local hosts say helps them keep up with the rising cost of living and pay increasingly high property taxes, the spokesperson said.

Over a third of nights booked on Airbnb last year were for stays of 30 days or longer, the largest share of any stay length which are longer stays are often tied to medical care, school or work relocations, or emergencies, per company data.

Listings for entire homes in the ward make up roughly 1 percent of ward’s housing stock, and most local hosts share their space only occasionally, with 78 percent sharing their home fewer than 90 nights a year and 18 percent sharing only a private room, according to the company.

“I can completely acknowledge that the revenue helps particularly small landlords keep up with the increased cost of property taxes and we can also acknowledge that those are units that don’t go to residents that want to live in this community,” Fuentes said. “Renting to residents can also bring in revenue to be able to pay the property taxes.”

While the Airbnb referendum is just a way to get feedback before any policy materializes, the bigger issue remains the need to build more housing, especially lower-cost housing, Fuentes said. Fuentes also said it was important to address rising property taxes to help keep longtime residents in their homes and have apartments for those fighting to stay in the area.

“The Airbnb limitation is not the only thing that I want to hear from constituents on — I want to make sure folks are coming into my office and asking for the support they need on [property tax] appeals while we are advocating for a more fair policy on property taxes across the state,” Fuentes said.

Early voting is now open for 26th Ward residents at Humboldt Park Library, 1605 N. Troy St.
